analyses.title: Topic Detection and Tracking Evaluation Overview
analyses.research_question: How can topic detection and tracking technologies for multilingual news streams be defined and evaluated consistently under controlled conditions?
analyses.methodology: The chapter presents the Topic Detection and Tracking evaluation framework rather than proposing a single detection algorithm. It describes controlled laboratory simulations built around shared LDC TDT corpora and common evaluation metrics. The framework separates the problem into Topic Tracking, Link Detection, Topic Detection, First Story Detection, and Story Segmentation tasks.

key_findings.finding: Topic continuity in a document stream can be decomposed into five distinct evaluation tasks: tracking, link detection, topic detection, first-story detection, and story segmentation.
TDT uses controlled laboratory simulations so competing technologies can be compared under standardized conditions.
Shared corpora and evaluation metrics are central components of the TDT methodology.
The evaluation framework is designed for multilingual, news-oriented textual material originating from multiple broadcast-news sources.

limitations: The accessible source is an abstract-level overview, so detailed metric definitions and experimental results could not be inspected.
The framework is centered on broadcast and news streams rather than workplace communication such as email or chat.
The evaluation uses controlled laboratory simulations rather than longitudinal deployment in real communication systems.
The chapter primarily defines an evaluation methodology and does not present a new topic-tracking model.
raw_claims: TDT was designed to support technologies that organize and search streams of news-oriented material.
The program evaluates systems through controlled laboratory simulations.
Common TDT corpora provide shared material for comparative evaluation.
The evaluation methodology includes explicit performance metrics.
Topic Tracking and Link Detection are treated as separate research tasks.
Topic Detection, First Story Detection, and Story Segmentation are also evaluated independently.

analyses.title: Cross-document Event Identity via Dense Annotation
analyses.research_question: How can cross-document event identity be densely annotated so that both full event identity and important forms of partial or quasi-identity are represented?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct related storylines from English Wikinews and automatically extract open-domain event mentions, followed by expert correction. Crowd workers then inspect pairs of documents and densely link event mentions across the pair, with follow-up questions about overlap in time, location, participants, and event inclusion. The resulting CDEC-WN corpus is analyzed for different kinds of partial identity, and two mention-pair baselines, including a neural cross-encoder, are evaluated on held-out subtopics. The study deliberately represents coreference as pairwise links rather than forcing all links into transitive event clusters.

key_findings.finding: CDEC-WN contains 7,220 event mentions and 4,282 cross-document event links across 198 document pairs drawn from 55 subtopics.
About 32 percent of the annotated cross-document links were identified as candidates for partial rather than full event identity.
The analysis identifies membership, subevent relations, and a newly proposed spatiotemporal-continuity category as important forms of quasi-identity.
Partial event identity can violate transitivity, making conventional event clustering an imperfect representation for these links.
The neural cross-encoder reaches 57.6 test F1 compared with 48.2 for the lemma-matching baseline, but performance remains limited, particularly on partial identity.
The corpus contains substantially denser event annotation per document than several earlier cross-document event-coreference resources.

limitations: The corpus is limited to English Wikinews.
The released study focuses on the Disasters and Accidents domain.
The annotation covers cross-document relations but does not add within-document event coreference.
The authors acknowledge that some coreference links may be missing or incorrect despite quality-control procedures.
The baseline evaluation assumes gold event mentions and known subtopics.
The pairwise representation accommodates non-transitive quasi-identity but does not directly produce globally coherent event clusters.
raw_claims: CDEC-WN was built from English Wikinews articles grouped into related storylines.
The corpus contains 176 documents organized into 198 cross-document pairs.
Its 7,220 event mentions participate in 4,282 annotated cross-document links.
The annotations distinguish 2,914 full-coreference links from 1,368 partial-identity links.
Annotators record whether linked events overlap in participants, time, and location.
Membership and subevent relations are recurring forms of partial event identity.
Spatiotemporal continuity is proposed as another form of quasi-identity.
The authors avoid mandatory clustering because partial identity is not always transitive.
A cross-encoder outperforms a lemma-based baseline but still has difficulty with partial identity.

analyses.title: Using a sledgehammer to crack a nut? Lexical diversity and event coreference resolution
analyses.research_question: Is EventCorefBank representative of the lexical and event diversity found in large news streams, and can its coverage be improved by adding distinct instances of the same event types?
analyses.methodology: The authors assess the representativeness of EventCorefBank with respect to the broader population of high-volume news. They find that its domains usually center on a single seminal event and therefore augment it with 502 additional texts describing different instances of event types already present in its 43 topics. The augmented resource is released as ECB+ for subsequent event-coreference research.

key_findings.finding: EventCorefBank generally covers only one seminal event within a domain, substantially simplifying the diversity encountered in real news streams.
Introducing different instances of already represented event types increases the corpus's lexical and event diversity.
The augmentation adds 502 texts spanning alternative instances associated with the 43 existing ECB topics.
The resulting ECB+ corpus is intended to provide a more representative resource for event-coreference research on web news.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible, so detailed experimental procedures and quantitative analyses could not be verified.
The corpus remains focused on news rather than workplace communication.
The augmentation is organized around the 43 event-topic domains already represented in ECB rather than unrestricted open-domain communication.
The accessible abstract does not report downstream coreference-system performance on the augmented corpus.
raw_claims: EventCorefBank is used as an evaluation resource for event coreference.
Its original topic domains usually concentrate on one seminal event.
That structure understates the event and lexical diversity of broader news streams.
The authors add 502 texts describing alternative instances of existing event types.
The expansion covers event types associated with the 43 existing ECB topics.
The augmented resource is released as ECB+ for further research.

analyses.title: WEC: Deriving a Large-scale Cross-document Event Coreference dataset from Wikipedia
analyses.research_question: Can Wikipedia hyperlink structure be exploited to build a large corpus-wide cross-document event-coreference dataset efficiently and support models beyond the topic-partitioned setting of earlier corpora?
analyses.methodology: The authors identify Wikipedia pages representing events and use hyperlinks whose anchors point to the same event page as candidate coreferent mentions, followed by several automatic filters. The English training set is generated automatically, while development and test clusters are manually validated. They train a RoBERTa-based mention-pair model followed by agglomerative clustering and evaluate it with standard coreference metrics on WEC and ECB+. They also perform cross-corpus training and testing to measure differences between the two resources.

key_findings.finding: The WEC English training set contains 40,529 event mentions grouped into 7,042 clusters, providing substantially larger-scale supervision than earlier manually built datasets.
Unlike topic-partitioned corpora, WEC permits mentions to corefer across the corpus rather than restricting links to predefined topic clusters.
Manual checking of development and test data yielded estimated annotation precision of 0.95, recall of 0.96, and Cohen's kappa of 0.75 in the reported quality check.
The proposed model achieves 62.3 CoNLL F1 on WEC compared with 53.1 for the lemma baseline, a 9.2-point improvement.
On ECB+, the same modeling approach reaches 80.8 CoNLL F1, exceeding the cited Joint baseline at 79.5.
Cross-corpus transfer loses roughly 8 to 12 CoNLL-F1 points, showing that WEC and ECB+ encode materially different event-mention distributions and corpus structures.
A manual sample indicates that WEC is dominated by referential and nominal event mentions, whereas ECB+ contains more descriptive and verbal mentions.

limitations: The training portion is automatically derived and therefore contains annotation noise; only development and test data are manually validated.
Event-mention annotation is not exhaustive, and the experiments evaluate clustering over gold mentions.
The presented corpus is derived from English Wikipedia and adaptation to other languages requires language-specific resources such as NER and event-page identification.
Wikipedia hyperlinking introduces selection and lexical biases that require filtering and downsampling of repeated mention strings.
WEC primarily captures referential Wikipedia mentions, which differ from the more descriptive event mentions common in news corpora.
The baseline sometimes fails to exploit contextual time and location evidence and has difficulty with longer mention spans.
raw_claims: WEC derives candidate event-coreference clusters from hyperlinks pointing to Wikipedia event pages.
Its English training split contains 40,529 mentions in 7,042 clusters.
Coreference links are not restricted to predefined topic partitions.
Development and test clusters are manually validated while training data remain automatically generated.
The WEC model reaches 62.3 CoNLL F1 compared with 53.1 for a lemma baseline.
The same model reaches 80.8 CoNLL F1 on ECB+.
Models trained on one corpus perform substantially worse when transferred to the other corpus.
WEC contains many referential nominal mentions that differ from the descriptive event mentions prevalent in ECB+.
The authors release the dataset and implementation for further research.

analyses.title: Generalizing Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution Across Multiple Corpora
analyses.research_question: How well do cross-document event-coreference systems and their learned signals generalize across heterogeneous corpora, and can multi-corpus evaluation and training improve robustness?
analyses.methodology: The authors establish a uniform evaluation across ECB+, GVC, and a token-level reannotation of FCC called FCC-T. They compare a corpus-independent feature-based mention-pair system with a recent neural event-coreference model and analyze which action, participant, temporal, spatial, and contextual features matter in each corpus. They then train systems on individual and combined corpora and test cross-corpus transfer using coreference metrics including LEA and CoNLL measures. Model behavior and dataset structure are also inspected to identify sources of corpus-specific overfitting.

key_findings.finding: Systems trained on a single event-coreference corpus suffer substantial performance degradation when evaluated on unseen corpora.
ECB+ can be modeled largely from event-action information, while FCC-T and GVC require a more balanced use of time, participants, and other contextual signals.
The feature-based approach has lower peak performance in some settings but behaves more consistently across corpora than the evaluated neural system.
Design choices tailored to ECB+, including exploiting its document-link distribution through preclustering, can overfit that corpus and generalize poorly elsewhere.
Joint training on FCC-T and GVC obtains a harmonic-mean LEA F1 of 40.9 across the evaluated corpora, more than 4.5 points above the best corresponding single-corpus training result.
The experiments support evaluating cross-document event-coreference systems on multiple corpora rather than treating strong performance on one benchmark as evidence of general robustness.

limitations: The empirical study is restricted to the news domain.
The evaluated corpora each contain fewer than one thousand documents, far below the scale of many real document streams.
The available corpora do not permit a meaningful investigation of event-coreference links across unrelated topic partitions.
The study evaluates three corpora and a limited set of system architectures, so conclusions about all possible modeling approaches remain bounded by that setup.
The authors do not demonstrate the effect of improved cross-document event coreference on downstream applications.
Incomplete event-mention annotation in existing corpora complicates end-to-end event-detection evaluation.
raw_claims: Prior cross-document event-coreference systems were commonly developed and evaluated on only one corpus.
The study compares ECB+, GVC, and the reannotated FCC-T corpus under a uniform setup.
Event-action similarity dominates prediction on ECB+ more strongly than on the other two datasets.
Time and participant information are more important on FCC-T and GVC.
Single-corpus models generally transfer poorly to unseen datasets.
A simpler feature-based model is more stable across corpora than the evaluated neural model.
Some ECB+-specific modeling choices exploit structural properties that do not transfer reliably.
Training on FCC-T and GVC together improves aggregate robustness across corpora.
The authors recommend multi-corpus evaluation for future cross-document event-coreference systems.
The released resources include data, annotation guidelines, and a system implementation.
